title: E-Commerce

pattern.summary: 8–10 questions, attempt any 5, each carries 20 marks. All theory, with many 'distinguish between', 'comment on' and 'short notes' questions (4–5 parts of 4–5 marks). Use Indian examples: UPI, Flipkart, Digital India, GeM.

choosing: Cyber law (IT Act 2000 and the 2008 amendment, offences and penalties) and e-payments (NEFT, RTGS, IMPS, UPI, payment gateways) come up in every paper.
Website hosting and web server vs application server are asked almost every session — short, easy marks.
The 'distinguish between' questions reuse the same pairs: Internet vs WWW, Windows vs Linux, symmetric vs asymmetric encryption, digital vs electronic signature.

topics.name: IT Act, Cyber Crime & Cyber Forensics
topics.summary: IT Act 2000 and the 2008 amendment, offences and punishments, penalties and adjudication, Appellate Tribunal, cyber crimes, cyber forensics, cyber terrorism.
points: IT Act, 2000: legal recognition of electronic records and digital signatures, e-governance, certifying authorities, offences and penalties; based on the UNCITRAL Model Law.

IT (Amendment) Act, 2008: technology-neutral 'electronic signature', data protection (Sec 43A — compensation for failing to protect sensitive data), new offences (Sec 66B–66F: receiving stolen computer resources, identity theft, cheating by personation, violation of privacy, cyber terrorism; Sec 66A on offensive messages was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015), child pornography (67B), intermediary liability (79), CERT-In's role.

Offences: tampering with source code (Sec 65), computer-related offences/hacking (66), identity theft (66C), cheating by personation (66D), privacy violation (66E), cyber terrorism (66F — up to life imprisonment), publishing obscene material (67).
Penalties and adjudication: compensation for damage to computer systems (Sec 43), adjudicating officers for claims; appeals to the Appellate Tribunal (now TDSAT), then the High Court.
Cyber crime: crime using a computer or network — hacking, phishing, identity theft, cyber stalking, cyber bullying, online fraud, ransomware, child pornography, cyber terrorism.
Cyber forensics: identifying, preserving, analysing and presenting digital evidence (hard disks, logs, mobiles) for use in court; electronic evidence may not be visible to an ordinary user.
topics.frame: Meaning → sections as headed points (section number + offence + punishment) → conclusion.
mistakes: Mixing up IT Act 2000 and 2008 — list what the amendment added.

topics.name: E-Payments & E-Banking
topics.summary: Types of electronic payment, EFT/NEFT/RTGS/IMPS/UPI, payment gateways, e-wallets, e-banking, online fund transfer, e-payment vs traditional payment.
points: Electronic payment systems: cards (credit, debit, prepaid), net banking, e-wallets (Paytm), UPI, EFT systems (NEFT, RTGS, IMPS), mobile banking, e-cheques.
EFT: electronic transfer from one account to another within or across banks.

NEFT: batch-wise settlement, no minimum, 24×7. RTGS: real-time gross settlement, one by one, minimum ₹2 lakh. IMPS: instant, 24×7, via mobile/net banking. UPI: instant real-time payments using a virtual payment address (VPA), linked to bank accounts.

Payment gateway: bridge between customer, merchant and banks that authorises online payments. Hosted (customer redirected to the gateway page — PayPal) vs self-hosted/integrated (payment on the merchant's site — more control, more security responsibility).

Online fund transfer requirements: bank account with net/mobile banking, beneficiary details (name, account number, IFSC), registered mobile for OTP, internet access; tools: net banking, mobile app, UPI app.
E-banking: banking over the internet — 24×7, lower costs, convenience; risks: fraud, phishing.
E-payment vs traditional payment: instant, trackable, no cash handling vs cash/cheque, slower; limits — cyber risk and need for connectivity vs theft, forgery.
Credit card (bank credit, pay later) vs e-wallet (prepaid balance stored in an app).
Other banking technology in the book: Automated Clearing House (bulk, recurring payments such as salaries and EMIs) and ATMs, POS terminals and mobile banking.
topics.frame: Meaning → types as headed points → comparison table (NEFT/RTGS/IMPS/UPI) → conclusion.

topics.name: Websites, Hosting & Web Servers
topics.summary: Website types and development, web hosting and its types, web server vs application server, HTTP vs HTTPS, Internet vs WWW.
points: Website: collection of related web pages under one domain. Types: static vs dynamic; personal, business/corporate, e-commerce, blog, portfolio, informational, social media, educational.
Web development process: information gathering → planning (sitemap) → design → content writing → coding → testing → launch → maintenance.
Web hosting: storing a website on a server connected to the internet. Types: shared, VPS, dedicated, cloud, managed WordPress, reseller, colocation.
Web server: serves static content over HTTP (Apache, Nginx). Application server: runs business logic and dynamic content (Tomcat, JBoss).
HTTP: unencrypted, port 80. HTTPS: encrypted with SSL/TLS, port 443, needed for payments.

Internet: the global network of networks. WWW: a service on the internet — linked web pages accessed by browsers. Evolution: Web 1.0 (read-only), Web 2.0 (interactive, social), Web 3.0 (semantic, decentralised).
A mail server stores and delivers e-mail; web server hardware ranges from a single machine to server farms and cloud instances, chosen by traffic, storage and uptime needs.
topics.frame: Meaning → types or steps as headed points → comparison table → conclusion.

topics.name: E-Tailing & E-Services
topics.summary: E-tailing and its models, 7 Cs of e-retail mix, e-services, e-publishing, online entertainment, e-learning and SWAYAM, OTT.
points: E-tailing: selling goods to consumers online. Models: pure-play (Amazon), brick-and-click (Reliance Digital), direct sales by manufacturer (D2C), marketplace, subscription.

Advantages for retailers: wider reach, lower costs, 24×7, customer data. For buyers: convenience, variety, price comparison, home delivery. Disadvantages: no touch and feel, delivery delays, returns, fraud risk.

7 Cs of the e-retail mix (Rayport and Jaworski's customer interface): context (site layout and design), content (products and information), community (reviews, user interaction), customisation (personalised pages), communication (messages to customers), connection (links to other sites), commerce (cart, payment, order tracking).
E-services: services delivered online (banking, ticketing, education, government). Advantages: speed, 24×7, lower cost, transparency.
E-publishing: publishing e-books, e-journals and news online; approaches — self-publishing, online platforms (Kindle), print-on-demand, open access.
Online entertainment and OTT: streaming platforms (Netflix, Hotstar) delivering content over the internet.
E-learning: learning over the internet. SWAYAM: Government of India's free MOOC platform with credit transfer.
topics.frame: Meaning → models or advantages as headed points with examples → conclusion.

topics.name: E-Commerce & Business Models
topics.summary: B2B, B2C, C2C, D2C, P2P and other models; business and revenue models; e-auctions, drop shipping, labelling; how major players work.
points: Transaction models: B2B (IndiaMART), B2C (Amazon), C2C (OLX, eBay), C2B, B2G (GeM), D2C (brands selling directly — boAt), P2P (peer-to-peer lending or sharing).
Business model elements: value proposition, revenue model, market opportunity, competitive environment, competitive advantage, market strategy, organisational development, management team.
Revenue models: advertising, subscription, transaction fee/commission, sales, affiliate.
E-auction: online real-time bidding (forward auction to sell, reverse auction to buy from pre-qualified suppliers).
Drop shipping: seller does not stock goods; the supplier ships directly to the customer.
Private labelling (product made for and sold under the retailer's brand) vs white labelling (generic product rebranded by many sellers).
App-based vs web-based business: mobile-first, push notifications vs browser-based, wider reach.

How players work: Flipkart/Amazon (marketplace + logistics), BigBasket (online grocery with warehouses), Zomato (restaurant aggregator and delivery), BookMyShow (ticketing), FirstCry (baby products, online + stores), eBay (C2C auctions).
topics.frame: Meaning → models with one Indian example each (a table) → merits and limits → conclusion.

topics.name: Cyber Security & Threats
topics.summary: Cyber security and its types and trends, threats and malware, spoofing, sniffing, phishing, internet vulnerabilities, cyber-physical systems.
points: Cyber security: protecting systems, networks and data from digital attacks. Information security protects all information (paper and digital); cyber security focuses on cyberspace.
Types/categories: network, application, information/data, cloud, endpoint, operational security, disaster recovery, user education.
Trends: AI-driven attacks and defence, ransomware, IoT vulnerabilities, cloud security, zero-trust, mobile threats, remote-work risks.
Malware: virus, worm, Trojan, ransomware, spyware, adware, rootkit, keylogger.
Spoofing: disguising as a trusted source. Sniffing: capturing data travelling on a network. Phishing: fake messages to steal credentials. Spyware: secretly monitors the user.
Internet vulnerabilities: weak passwords, unpatched software, insecure Wi-Fi, social engineering, misconfiguration.
Cyber-physical systems: computing controlling physical processes (smart grids, medical devices) — need security across sensors, networks and controllers.
Impact on e-commerce: builds trust, protects payments and customer data, avoids losses and legal liability.
topics.frame: Meaning → types or threats as headed points with examples → prevention → conclusion.

topics.name: E-Governance & Digital India
topics.summary: E-governance vs e-government, Gartner's four-phase model, India's e-governance journey, Digital India and its nine pillars, e-NAM, GeM, MyGov.
points: E-government: using ICT to deliver government services. E-governance: wider — ICT for government, citizens and businesses to interact, making governance transparent and participative.

Gartner's model: Phase 1 information (publish information online), Phase 2 interaction (downloadable forms, e-mail), Phase 3 transaction (pay bills, file returns online), Phase 4 transformation (integrated, citizen-centric services).
India's journey: 1990s computerisation (NIC, railway reservation), 2006 National e-Governance Plan (Mission Mode Projects), 2015 Digital India, then Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker, UMANG.

Digital India (2015) aims: digital infrastructure, governance and services on demand, digital empowerment. Nine pillars: broadband highways, universal mobile access, public internet access, e-governance, e-Kranti, information for all, electronics manufacturing, IT for jobs, early harvest programmes.
e-NAM: online national agricultural market. GeM: Government e-Marketplace for public procurement. MyGov: citizen participation platform.
E-commerce (business transactions for profit) vs e-governance (government services for citizens).
topics.frame: Meaning → phases or pillars as a numbered list → examples → conclusion.

topics.name: Operating Systems, SDLC & Apps
topics.summary: Operating systems (Windows vs Linux), software platforms, SDLC for e-commerce, app development, app stores, mobile frameworks.
points: Operating system: software that manages hardware and runs applications. Windows: proprietary, paid, user-friendly GUI. Linux: open source, free, secure, customisable, popular for servers.
Software platforms: desktop (Windows, macOS), mobile (Android, iOS), web, cloud (AWS), e-commerce platforms (Shopify, Magento, WooCommerce).
SDLC for e-commerce solutions: planning → requirement analysis → design → development → testing → deployment → maintenance.
App development process: idea and research → planning → UI/UX design → development (front end and back end) → testing → launch on app stores → updates.
App store: marketplace to distribute apps. Types: platform stores (Google Play, Apple App Store), third-party stores, enterprise stores.
Mobile development frameworks: native (Swift, Kotlin), cross-platform (Flutter, React Native), hybrid (Ionic).
E-commerce software for SMEs: ready-made storefronts, payment and inventory integration (Shopify, Dukaan).
topics.frame: Meaning → steps as a flow chart or comparison table → examples → conclusion.

topics.name: E-Commerce: Meaning, Evolution & Impact
topics.summary: Meaning, evolution, advantages and disadvantages, e-commerce vs traditional commerce and e-business, 24×7 service, impact of AI and IoT.
points: E-commerce: buying and selling goods and services over electronic networks. E-business is wider — all business processes online (supply chain, HR, CRM).
Evolution: EDI and EFT (1970s–80s) → WWW and early online stores (1990s) → dot-com boom → mobile and social commerce → AI-driven, omnichannel commerce.
Advantages: global reach, 24×7, lower costs, personalisation, easy comparison. Disadvantages: security and privacy concerns, no physical inspection, delivery and return problems, digital divide.
E-commerce vs traditional: online vs physical; 24×7 vs limited hours; global vs local; digital vs cash payments.
Architectural framework: network infrastructure, publishing and multimedia content, messaging, business services (security, payment), applications.
Emerging technologies: AI (recommendations, chatbots), IoT (smart devices ordering automatically), AR/VR, blockchain, big data.
topics.frame: Meaning → headed points (advantages vs disadvantages table) → conclusion.

topics.name: Encryption & Digital Signatures
topics.summary: Encryption, symmetric vs asymmetric, digital signature, electronic signature, digital signature certificates.
points: Encryption: converting plaintext into ciphertext so only authorised parties can read it; decryption reverses it.
Symmetric encryption: one shared key (fast; key-sharing problem — AES). Asymmetric: public key encrypts, private key decrypts (slower, secure key exchange — RSA).
Digital signature: created with the signer's private key and a hash of the document; verified with the public key — ensures authenticity, integrity and non-repudiation.
Electronic signature: any electronic means of signing (typed name, scanned signature, OTP-based e-Sign) — digital signature is a secure type of electronic signature.
Digital Signature Certificate (DSC): issued by a Certifying Authority under the IT Act; classes by level of verification; used for e-filing, MCA and GST filings, e-tenders.
topics.frame: Meaning → process diagram (sender signs with private key → receiver verifies with public key) → comparison table → conclusion.

topics.name: FinTech, DLT & Digital Currencies
topics.summary: FinTech and its technologies, distributed ledger technology, digital vs virtual vs crypto currencies.
points: FinTech: innovative use of technology to deliver financial services (Paytm, Zerodha, PhonePe).
Technologies: AI and machine learning, blockchain/DLT, cloud computing, big-data analytics, APIs/open banking, biometrics, robotic process automation.
Distributed ledger technology: a shared, replicated record across many nodes. Advantages: transparency, security, no single point of failure, faster settlement, lower costs.

Digital currency: any money in electronic form (includes central bank digital currency — the e-Rupee). Virtual currency: digital value issued by private developers, used in a specific community (game tokens). Cryptocurrency: decentralised virtual currency secured by cryptography (Bitcoin).
topics.frame: Meaning → headed points → comparison table → conclusion.
